STRONGLY TRADITIONAL

I Can Only Imagine 2

Overall Perspective

The first "I Can Only Imagine" was a bonafide miracle at the box office. Eighty-three million dollars on a budget that most Marvel movies spend on catering. Eight years later the Erwin Brothers are back with a sequel, and the question hanging over it is simple: can they do it again?

Short answer: not quite. But that's okay. This is still one of the safest bets for conservative families hitting theaters in 2026.

The film picks up with Bart Millard (John Michael Finley) stuck in a creative rut. MercyMe is still touring, still packing arenas, but Bart hasn't written anything close to the song that made him famous. His oldest son Sam (Sammy Dell) has been diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, and Bart's response is to wrap the kid in bubble wrap and smother him with worry. Meanwhile Milo Ventimiglia shows up as Tim Timmons, a real-life musician who opens for MercyMe and whose cancer diagnosis becomes the emotional gut punch of the whole movie. Dennis Quaid pops back in through flashbacks as Bart's deceased father Arthur, connecting this story to the redemption arc of the original.

The structure jumps around in time more than it needs to. There are stretches where the filmmakers can't seem to decide if this is Bart's story, Tim's story, or Sam's story. The concert sequences run long and occasionally feel like extended music videos for songs you can already stream. And yeah, Sam's diabetes subplot sometimes leans into melodrama that overstates how scary the condition is for a teenager who's managing it. Though to be fair, the film is showing us Bart's fear, not Sam's reality. Any parent who's watched their kid get a serious diagnosis will recognize that irrational protectiveness.

On the woke spectrum, this film is spotless. Zero. Nothing. Not a trace. There's no identity politics wedged into the narrative. The cast is diverse the way a real touring band's crew would be diverse. Nobody is checking boxes. Nobody is delivering speeches about representation. The film's worldview is unapologetically, unashamedly Christian. Prayer works here. Faith isn't deconstructed or treated with ironic distance. It's presented as the answer, full stop.

Where the movie genuinely shines is in how it handles suffering. Lesser faith films treat hardship as a speed bump on the way to a happy ending. This one lets the pain sit. Tim Timmons' cancer is not wrapped up in a neat bow. The film earns its tears instead of demanding them. Bart's arc from control freak to trusting father mirrors the spiritual message without beating you over the head with it. The marriage between Bart and Shannon (Sophie Skelton) is portrayed as genuinely loving but under real strain. That's so much more compelling than the perfect-marriage fantasy you get from most Christian films.

It's not as emotionally devastating as the original. It doesn't have that singular song-origin moment that made the first film unforgettable. But it's honest. And in 2026 that counts for a lot.

Adult Viewer Insight

Conservative adult viewers will find nothing to worry about here. The Erwin Brothers have a perfect track record of delivering sincere, faith-first content, and this sequel is no exception. The craft criticisms are real: the pacing drags in spots, the time-jumping structure can be disorienting, and it doesn't reach the emotional heights of the original. But the spiritual core is genuine, the performances are committed, and the treatment of suffering as a pathway to deeper faith rather than a reason to abandon it is refreshingly mature for the genre. This is one of the increasingly rare wide-release films that conservative families can attend without any ideological anxiety whatsoever.

Parental Guidance

This is an easy recommendation for families. No violence, no sexual content, no language concerns. The emotional intensity comes from a child's diabetes diagnosis, a friend's cancer journey, and the fear of losing people you love. Sensitive younger children may find the hospital scenes and discussions of mortality upsetting, but for most kids 8 and up this is perfectly appropriate. The film provides excellent conversation starters about trusting God through hardship, dealing with illness in the family, and the difference between protecting someone and controlling them.
